The Cebuano text never says hulmigas/olmigas anywhere, so a child reading only the Cebuano learns that a queen BIRD lives 20-30 years while its workers live weeks — false, and the actual ant fact is unrecoverable (only the untranslated English title_bis "Ant Queen Kinabuhi" hints at it). Note the same batch uses langgam correctly for birds in ffct-09192, confirming the Cebuano sense.

Body calls the tadpole `lawalawa`, which means SPIDER everywhere else in this corpus (ffct-00695, ffct-02002, ffct-00538). The Cebuano reads 'the spider's tail doesn't fall off when it becomes a frog... while its legs grow', so a Cebuano-only child learns spiders turn into frogs. Other tadpole cards use `tadpole` or `ulo-ulo` (ffct-01714, ffct-02027).

Sneeze card never says sneeze. title_bis "Mga Lakang sa Lawas sa Bahin" and the body "Sa dili ka mobahin..." use bahin (part/share/divide), not bahing (sneeze). Unlike the other sneeze cards in the corpus, nothing here restores the subject: the English "drive the irritant away" is also dropped, so the Cebuano is just deep breath + chest/belly muscles + air blasted out, which a child would read as breathing or hiccups. Note this is systematic (118 corpus cards use mobahin/pagbahin vs 17 with bahing), so the grep will be noisy — this card is the instance where the fact is unrecoverable.

title_bis "Liki sa Usa" = "crack in the deer"; the card is about fawn spots (body correctly uses batik). liki means crack/crevice everywhere else in the corpus (95 cards: cracked mud, bone fracture, rock crevices, fault lines), so it is wrong for "spots" in general. The title names a different thing than the card; the body does correct it.

title_bis "Lawas Ayaw Kaugalingon" for "The Body Repairs Itself": ayaw is the Cebuano prohibitive ("don't"), not ayo/pag-ayo (heal). In the same corpus ~55 titles use Ayaw correctly as "don't" (Ayaw Tan-aw sa Adlaw, Ayaw Langoy sa Baha), so a child reads this title as a prohibition rather than a statement that the body heals itself. Systematic in heal-titles (Panit Ayaw Samad, Mitosis Tubo Ayaw, Hinay Ayaw Samad, Suri Ayaw TB). Body sentence is correct.

Body calls the parrot "abuk" (= dust) in both the question line and the explanation, and it is the emphasized word: "Abuk o kalaw—kinsay motabang og tanom? Mobuak ug mokaon ang abuk sa liso...". Corpus-wide this bird is always "loro" (40+ cards); "abuk" appears nowhere else. Half the comparison (the seed-cracking parrot) is attached to a word meaning dust; only the English word "Parrot" in title_bis hints at the intended animal.

The Cebuano question is flipped but the answer word was kept, so the card contradicts itself. EN: "Are floating plants and algae the same?" / "No!". BIS: "Managlahi ba ang lumot ug naglutaw nga tanom?" (= are they DIFFERENT?) answered "Dili!" — i.e. "no, they are not different" = they are the same, the opposite of the fact. The following sentence then explains that they do differ, so the emphasized answer teaches the false belief.

title_bis "Langgam Baho Dalan" names a bird — in Cebuano langgam = bird (this same corpus uses langgam for birds, e.g. ffct-09598 "May ngipon ba ang mga langgam?"). The card is about ants and the body correctly says "hulmigas". Looks like a Tagalog carry-over (Tagalog langgam = ant) and it is systemic: ~30 ant cards across the sweep carry langgam titles over hulmigas bodies (ffct-00110, ffct-01749, ffct-02267, ffct-03925, ffct-08067, ffct-11146, ffct-13875, ...), so the grep is likely to be mostly true positives here.

The question line says "Ngano nga nagsidlak ang lambay sa gagamba sa buntag?" — lambay is a crab, not a web (elsewhere in this corpus: "Ang kugita mokaon og lambay, pasayan, ug kinhason"). Other web cards use sapot / lawa / lambat. The thing the dew sticks to is misnamed as a different animal in the question the child has to answer; only title_bis ("Tun-og sa Lawa") carries the correct word.

The damselfly is named `kasing-kasing`, which is Cebuano for HEART (the corpus uses kasing-kasing for the heart organ everywhere else, e.g. the ECG card). Body: 'Unsaon pag-ila sa alindahaw gikan sa kasing-kasing? ... nagkalayo ang mata sa kasing-kasing.' Nothing in the card corrects it: title_bis is 'Tutubi ug Damselfly' (Tagalog tutubi + English damselfly), so there is zero lexical overlap with the body's alindahaw/kasing-kasing pair and the mapping is only positional, and the wrong word is also pushed into emph_bis. A child reading only the Cebuano learns that a 'heart' is an insect with wide-set eyes and cannot tell a damselfly from a dragonfly. Other cards in the corpus render damselfly as plain 'damselfly' or 'nipis nga alindahaw' (ffct-04554, ffct-14224), so this is a one-off mistranslation, not a regional name.

title_bis "Pagkaon sa Siga" = "Food of the Flame" — siga is flame/light in Cebuano, not a fish. The card is Mudskipper Diet, and the title never names the mudskipper, so the header tells a child the card is about something else entirely. Corpus check: siga appears ~40x elsewhere only as flame/light (Siga sa Aninipot = firefly light, Siga sa Anglerfish, Kolor sa Siga sa Bunsen Burner), and every other mudskipper card uses tambasakan, baklaw, or mudskipper. Same pattern as the known cat-card-titled-iro defect.

EN 'ran experiments with pea plants' -> BIS 'nagbuhat og mga eksperimento sa mga sitaw'. 'Sitaw' is string bean, a different plant: this same corpus says 'gisantes' for Mendel's peas in every other card (ffct-03787, ffct-04092, ffct-04392, ffct-08276, dcard-01613, ffct-38435) and reserves 'sitaw' for string beans (ffct-05422, ffct-00127). The correct word appears only in title_bis ('Gisantes ni Mendel'), so the Cebuano body teaches that genetics was discovered on string beans. Same shape as the gold-set tabanog/dragonfly flag (ffct-08595).

EN 'white, feathery flowers on top that sway gently whenever the wind blows' -> BIS 'bulak sa tumoy nga nag-alindahaw kon adunay hangin'. 'Alindahaw' is this corpus's word for DRAGONFLY (25 cards: ffct-00093, ffct-01239, ffct-04274, ffct-05044...), never a verb for swaying; elsewhere it is glossed as drizzle. The swaying-in-the-wind action is the second half of the card and is never stated any other way, so a Cebuano-only child cannot say what the plumes do in the wind.

title_en 'Forests Feed the Rain' -> title_bis 'Kagsuban nga Minus sa Ulan'. 'Kagsuban' is this corpus's title word for forest (ffct-04015, ffct-07403, ffct-14604) and the frame 'X nga Minus sa Y' means 'X reduces Y' elsewhere (ffct-05803 'Sweat Reduces Urine' -> 'Bahu nga Minus sa Ihi'). So the child-facing title asserts forests REDUCE rain, the reverse of the card, whose body correctly says cutting forests lowers local rainfall. Body is correct; the title states the opposite relationship.

title_en 'Cloud Rat Pale Belly Fur' -> title_bis 'Lumot Tiyan Cloud Rat'. 'Lumot' is moss/algae in all 167 other corpus uses (48 titles, 119 bodies) with no exception, so the title tells a child the cloud rat has moss on its belly. Same class as the gold-set title entity-swaps 'Toxic Asin Plastik' (ffct-15087) and 'Agta' for mold (ffct-10181). Honest caveat: the body is intact ('mas humok ug mas mapusok nga balhibo... lahi ang kolor'), and 'Lumot' could be a one-letter slip for 'lumo' (soft), so this is lower confidence than the three above.

Ant queen card: the Cebuano says "Ang reyna nga langgam" — in Cebuano langgam is a BIRD (the Tagalog false friend langgam = ant). The card never says hulmigas anywhere, and the workers are only "mga trabahante", so a Cebuano child reads this as a queen bird being fed mouth-to-mouth by workers. The whole ant-colony fact is unrecoverable. Corpus check confirms the correct word is used elsewhere ("Ants" -> "Hulmigas", 001.json) and that the same bird/ant slip recurs (000.json "Ants Per Person" -> "Langgam sa Matag Tawo").

Gecko-on-wet-surface card: "makasagabal ang tubig sa pagbira sa mga balahibo sa bungbong" puts the hairs on the WALL (bungbong), not on the gecko's toes. The card never mentions tudlo/toes, so the mechanism a child takes away is that walls have hairs — false, and not restored anywhere on the card. Compare ffct-10137 in the same batch, which correctly puts the balhibo "sa ilalom sa iyang mga tudlo". Not giving a general word pair: bungbong is the right word for wall, the defect is where the hairs were attached.

title_bis "Peacock sa Pagyugyog sa Buhok" renders feathers as buhok (human head hair); Cebuano for feathers is balhibo. The body only says "Iuyog niini ang ikog" and never says balhibo, so feathers are never restored — the title asserts a peacock shakes its hair. Lower severity than the other two (the body still delivers tail-shake -> rattling sound -> peahen hears it), but the wrong word is wrong in general. Note this looks systematic in titles corpus-wide (027.json "Buhok nga Motabon sa Langgam", 031.json "Buhok sa Lupad sa Langgam", 160.json "Buhok sa Hangin"), while 074.json correctly uses "Balhibo sa Langgam" — so a grep will hit many real instances, not noise.

Sharks-in-danger card: EN 'especially just for their fins' becomes 'ilabi na para lang sa ilang mga kapikas' — kapikas means mate/partner (corpus uses it that way in 37 cards, e.g. ffct-00276, ffct-02433). Fins are palikpik/kapay everywhere else in the corpus (66 fin cards). A child reads that sharks are over-caught 'just for their mates'; the finning fact is destroyed and nothing in the card restores it.

MMR card: 'nanalipod batok niini, ug usab sa baki ug German measles'. baki = frog/toad in this corpus (185 cards, incl. ffct-10459 in this same batch). Mumps is rendered beke everywhere else (ffct-00400 'mumps (beke)', ffct-02413 titled 'Beke'). The card never says beke/mumps, so the child learns MMR protects against measles, frogs and German measles — one of the three diseases is lost.

title_bis 'Toxoplasma Iro Busug' for EN 'Toxoplasma Cats Pregnancy': iro = dog, but the card is about cats (body correctly says pusa), and busug = full/satiated, not pregnant (buntis/mabdos). The title asserts the wrong animal for the parasite risk — same defect class as the known cat-card-titled-iro example.

title_bis 'Makahiya nga Layo sa Pilipinas' for EN 'Wild Makahiya Everywhere': layo = far/distant, which asserts the opposite of the card's point (makahiya is easy to find, grows along roadsides and yards). 'Wild' (ihalas, as used in the parallel card ffct-10539) is also gone. Title makes a false claim about where makahiya is found.

Plant bulb rendered as 'bombilya' (electric light bulb) in BOTH title_bis ('Bumbilya Asukar Dahon') and body ('Unsa ba gyud ang gitipig sulod sa bombilya? Ang pagkaon nga gitipig sa bombilya...'). Nothing in the Cebuano names a plant part, so a child reads that sugar and starch are stored inside a light bulb. The English is about an onion-type storage bulb. Unrecoverable from the card.

EN 'winding ridges and grooves on its surface' becomes 'liko-liko nga mga tubo ug kinhason sa ibabaw niini'. 'Kinhason' is shellfish/seashells, a completely different thing, and 'tubo' (pipe) is not a ridge. The card asserts brain coral has shellfish on its surface and never corrects it; only the 'looks like a brain' part survives.

title_bis 'Schisto Dali Hawak' reads as schisto being easily caught by touch/contact - the exact myth the card exists to debunk (title_en: 'Schisto Not by Touch'). Looks like 'Dili' corrupted to 'Dali'; also 'hawak' is waist in Cebuano, not touch (hikap/gunit, as the body uses). Body does say 'Dili!', so a full reader recovers it, but the heading alone states the opposite health claim.

title_bis 'Anemone sa Ermitanyo' translates 'hermit crab' as 'ermitanyo' - a hermit/recluse person, not an animal. Body correctly says 'umang', so the fact is recoverable, but the title names a different thing (same class as the cat card titled 'iro').

Body uses Tagalog 'buto' for bone twice ('hawan ang buto niini', 'gaan nga buto'). Cebuano for bone is 'bukog' (which title_bis correctly uses); Cebuano 'buto' means explode / seed / vulgar genitals, so the question 'Molutaw ba ang langgam tungod kay hawan ang buto niini?' names a different thing in a kids' card. Title restores the fact, so lower severity, but the swap is wrong for Cebuano in general.

EN: "...all work together to break down food and absorb nutrients"; BIS: "...magkauban nga nagpurito sa pagkaon ug nagsuyop og sustansya". `purito` is not a word in this corpus at all (0 of 49,156 cards; the corpus renders "break down food" as pagtunaw / magbungkag / pagdugmok / naglata across 52 cards), and the nearest reading for a child is `prito` = fried, so the Cebuano body says the mouth, esophagus, stomach and intestines FRY the food. The tl row has it right ("nagtutunaw ng pagkain"), so this is bis-specific. Partial mitigation: title_bis "Sistema sa Paghilis" still says digestion, so a child may recover the topic but not the mechanism.

EN: "Why are pitcher plants so brightly colored? Pitchers are often brightly colored like flowers so they can attract insects more easily." BIS: "Ngano nga mabulokon ang mga tabo? Ang mga tabo kasagaran mabulokon nga morag bulak aron mas madani ang mga insekto." The Cebuano never says tanom / pitcher plant anywhere in the body — the subject is only ever "tabo", which to a Cebuano child is the water dipper (or a market day, tabo-an). The English question line anchors it with "pitcher plants"; the Cebuano question line drops that anchor. The only other anchor is title_bis "Nepenthes", a Latin name a grade-5 child will not know. Corpus check: 34 pitcher-plant cards use "tabo" only for the cup and always with "pitcher plant" / "tanom" adjacent in the same sentence (e.g. "sa sulod sa tabo sa pitcher plant") — this card is the one where the anchor is missing, so the child is told dippers are brightly coloured to attract insects. Slug not a word-pair, because "tabo" for the cup itself is fine when anchored.

title_bis "Langgam Salag Ilalom" on an ants card (title_en "Ants Underground Nests"). In Cebuano langgam = BIRD (705 cards in the corpus use it that way); ant is hulmigas/hantik, which is what this card's own body correctly uses. The title as displayed says "Bird Nest Underground" — same shape as the known cat-card-titled-iro defect. Corpus-wide this is a systematic Tagalog false-friend leak: 47 of 147 ant cards carry langgam, several in the BODY where nothing restores it (ffct-07494 "Pila ka langgam ang mahimong mopuyo sa usa ka kolonya?", ffct-13875 "Reyna sa Langgam ... mga trabahante nga langgam", ffct-04685 "manggagawang langgam mga babaye nga langgam"), so the grep pattern should pay off well beyond this card.

title_bis "Tuko Dili Tuka sa Platypus" for title_en "Venom Spur Not Bill". In Cebuano tuko = GECKO — the corpus itself uses tuko as gecko in 53 cards ("Tiil sa Tuko", "Tuko vs Butiki"), and renders spur as "tibo", including in this card's own answer ("ang hilo niini naa sa hait nga tibo sa likod sa iyang tiil") and in the sibling platypus cards ("Tibo Platypus Kirot", "Venom Spur Platypus"). The title therefore reads "Gecko Not Beak of the Platypus" — a different animal named on the card. Same defect recurs in ffct-* "Echidna nga Tuko Walay Hilo" (Echidna's Harmless Spur), so spur->tuko is wrong in general, not a one-off.

Whole card swaps ants for birds. EN 'Why do ants walk in a line?' -> BIS 'Ngano nagsunod-sunod paglakaw ang mga langgam?' and 'Ang ubang langgam mosunod niini nga baho'; title_bis 'Baho nga Dalan sa Langgam'. In Cebuano langgam = BIRD (Tagalog false friend: langgam = ant). Only the stray English 'worker ant' hints otherwise, so a Cebuano-only reader learns birds follow scent trails in single file. Corpus elsewhere uses the correct 'hulmigas' (ffct-11049).

EN: termite soldiers defend the colony 'from predators like ants'. BIS: 'gikan sa mga manunukob sama sa langgam' = predators like BIRDS. The named predator is a different animal and nothing in the card corrects it.

Cat card titled with the word for dog: title_bis 'Iro Dila Balahibo' (dog/tongue/fur) for title_en 'Cats Groom Themselves'. The body correctly uses 'iring', but the title itself names the wrong animal - the same defect class already confirmed in this corpus.

Butterfly life cycle listed as 'itlog, tangkong, pupa, alibangbang'. 'Tangkong' is water spinach (kangkong), not a caterpillar ('ulod'). The correct word appears nowhere on the card, so the larval stage is unrecoverable - a child reads a vegetable as a life-cycle stage. The frog list ('itlog, ulo-ulo, baki') is fine.

title_bis 'Colugo sa Ungo' for title_en 'Colugo, Cousin of Monkeys'. 'Ungo' is the aswang/witch-ghoul, a completely different thing from 'unggoy' (monkey). The body uses 'unggoy' correctly, but the title as displayed names a monster.

title_bis 'Animalia Gingharian Tawo' for title_en 'Animalia Kingdom Animals' - the title says the Animalia kingdom is HUMANS ('tawo') instead of animals ('mananap'). Body is correct ('gingharian sa mga mananap'), but the title names the wrong group.

title_bis 'Matabang Pagkaon sa Bile' for title_en 'Fatty Food Frees Bile'. In Cebuano 'matabang' means BLAND/insipid (cf. 'tubig-tabang' = freshwater in ffct-11128), the opposite of the trigger described; fatty is 'tambok', which the body does use. The title therefore states that bland food releases bile.

title_bis 'Tiki nga Layag' for title_en 'Sailfin Lizard'. 'Tiki' is the house gecko, a different animal from the sailfin lizard (ibid/layagan); the card's fact is that it reaches almost a metre with over half of that tail, which is false for a gecko. Body keeps the English name, so only the title misnames it.

title_bis "Langgam Buhat Bug-at" for "Ants Carry Heavy Loads": in Cebuano langgam = BIRD (Tagalog false friend for ant). The body correctly uses hulmigas (as does ffct-11181's title), so the title labels the card with the wrong animal.

title_bis "Lima ka Kasingkasing sa Buli" for "An Earthworm's Five Hearts": buli is not earthworm in Cebuano (buri palm / backside). The body uses the correct word wati, so the title names a different thing entirely.

title_bis "Buyog sa Singhot" for "Why Bees Die After Stinging": singhot = to sniff/smell, not to sting. The body uses motusok/tuslok correctly, so the fact survives, but the title states the wrong action.

title_bis "Millipede nga Dili Mokaon" (= does not EAT) for "Harmless Millipedes"; the body says dili kini mopaak (does not bite). The title asserts a separate false claim (millipedes don't eat) that nothing on the card corrects.

title_bis 'Langgam Lalaki dili Bantay' — in Cebuano langgam is BIRD (Tagalog false friend for ant). The card is about male ants; body correctly uses 'hulmigas', so the title names a different animal than the whole card.
title_bis 'Iro Iro Dalunggan' for 'Dog Cat Swivel Ears' — says dog twice; the cat (iring) is gone, erasing the dog-vs-cat contrast the card exists to make. Body is correct ('iro ug iring').
title_bis 'Larynx sa Iro ug Iro' — 'dogs and dogs' where the card is about dogs AND cats; body correctly says 'iro ug iring'. Same title defect as ffct-11324.
title_bis 'Baki Dili Tinga' — 'tinga' is food stuck between the teeth, not warts (kulugo). The title states a different, unrelated claim about frogs; body keeps English 'warts'.

title_bis 'Lunok ug Piso' — 'lunok' is the VERB to swallow/gulp, not the bird. The bird sense was mistranslated, so the title reads 'Gulping and Chicks'; the bird is never named in Cebuano in the title.

title_bis 'Kapok Dili Bulak' — 'bulak' is flower; cotton is 'gapas' (used correctly in the body). The title asserts a different claim ('kapok is not a flower') than the card's point (kapok is not cotton).

title_bis 'Dagger sa Pagliko' for 'Hedgehogs Curl Into Balls' — the animal is missing entirely and an unrelated noun ('dagger') stands in its place; nothing in the title points to a hedgehog curling up.

English card is about WASPS (title_bis correctly says 'Tambuboan'), but the whole Cebuano body says 'putyukan' = honeybee: 'Tanan ba nga putyukan peligroso?... Ang ubang matang sa putyukan gagmay kaayo ug halos dili makatukol — hinuon, motabang sila sa pagkaon sa peste sa tanom.' A child reading only the Cebuano learns that some BEES barely sting and eat plant pests — a false claim about bees, and the wasp fact is never delivered. putyukan = bee throughout this corpus (e.g. the drone card ffct-11481); wasp is tamboboan/putakti.

title_bis 'Worker Langgam Hukay' — in Cebuano langgam = BIRD, not ant. The card is about worker ants digging nests (body keeps the English 'worker ant', so the title is the only Cebuano name for the animal and it names a different animal). Same class as the known cat-titled-iro defect. NOTE: this ant->langgam swap is corpus-wide (~40 cards in this sweep, many in the body text, e.g. ffct-01426 'Ang mga langgam nagbiya og...'), so the grep will hit broadly and legitimately.

title_bis 'Kilay nga Babag sa Bahu' = 'eyebrow that blocks ODOR/smell' (bahu/baho = smell). English title is 'Eyebrows Block Sweat' and the point of the card is that eyebrows stop sweat from reaching the eyes. The body is correct ('gibabagan niini ang singot gikan sa agtang'), but the title as read alone states a different, nonsensical function.

Wrong insect. EN is about a CICADA growing wings (title_bis correctly says 'Sikada'), but the body asks 'Kanus-a magkapako ang kagang?' — and corpus-wide 'kagang' is this corpus's word for CRICKET (8 other cards, all EN 'cricket': ffct-00655, ffct-01825, ffct-01874, ffct-03568, ffct-03598, ffct-03727, ffct-04846, ffct-11910); cicada is rendered 'kuliglig' elsewhere (ffct-11786 in this same batch). In general Cebuano 'kagang' is also a small crab, so a child reading only the body can learn that a crab/cricket is the animal that grows wings as an adult. The body never names the cicada, so the intended subject is not recoverable from the Cebuano text itself.

title_bis "Langgam sa 50x nga Bug-aton" names a BIRD (Cebuano langgam = bird) for a card about ants lifting 50x their weight; the body correctly says hulmigas but the title a child reads announces the wrong animal and is never corrected. Tagalog false-friend leak (Tagalog langgam = ant). Same defect recurs corpus-wide: ffct-00110 title "Langgam sa Matag Tawo" (Ants Per Person) and ffct-01726 title "Langgam nga Habol" (Weaver Ants); ffct-01426 has it in the BODY ("Giunsa pagpangita og pagkaon sa langgam?" for ants). Grep must be triaged as en=ant + bis=langgam only — 705 langgam cards are legitimately about birds.

"Napukan kini sa glucose nga gamiton sa mga selula" — pukan/napukan is to fall or be felled (a tree, a person), not to break down/convert (matunaw, mabungkag, magub-a, which this corpus uses elsewhere). The card's mechanism step, carbohydrates BREAK DOWN INTO glucose, is destroyed; nothing else in the Cebuano restores it (title_bis is only "Carbohydrate Kusog"), so a Cebuano-only child gets carbs = energy and glycogen storage but never the carb->glucose conversion. Hapax: the only occurrence of napukan in the 47k-card sweep corpus.

Kapok seeds are said to be wrapped in 'humok nga puti nga BULAK' — bulak is flower in Cebuano (this is the Tagalog false friend bulak = cotton). The card never says fiber/lanot, so a Cebuano-only child reads that kapok seeds are wrapped in soft white flowers and that flowers are stuffed into pillows. Every other kapok card in the corpus uses lanot / hibla / lugas / balhibo; the CPT Cebuano corpus uses bulak exclusively for flower and gapas for cotton.

Blink card. title_bis '28000 Sukmol Adlaw' — sukmol is a punch/blow, not a blink; and the body never rescues it because it uses 'mokirok' (a word that appears exactly once in 47k cards and not at all in the Cebuano CPT corpus) instead of the standard pilok/pamilok/kurap used by ~30 other blink cards. So the card only says we do some unnamed thing 15-20 times a minute, 28,000 times a day.

title_bis 'Gamot sa Uga nga Dahon' names leaf ROOTS (gamot) for leaf VEINS; the body correctly uses ugat, so the title heads a leaf-vein card with a plant part leaves do not have. Same title-level swap recurs at ffct-04299 ('Gamot Dahon Daloy') and ffct-06538 ('Gamot sa Dahon sa Bagyo'), while 19 other leaf-vein cards title it 'Ugat sa Dahon'.

title_bis 'Paspas nga Signal sa Bali' — bali in Cebuano is a fracture/break (cf. ffct-02396 'First Aid sa Bali', ffct-02434 'Bali nga Bukog'), so the balance card is titled 'fast fracture signals'. Body correctly says balanse. Same truncation of balanse -> Bali also at ffct-01096 and ffct-01346.

English 'bats, birds, and bees pollinate flowers and spread seeds' becomes 'motabang sa pagpamulak sa bulak' = help the flowers BLOOM. Pollination is replaced by a different process and nothing in the card restores it (no polen/polinasyon), so the child learns that fruit-eating animals make flowers bloom. 26+ corpus cards use polinasyon/pollinate; the one other card that uses pagpamulak (ffct-07113) repairs it with 'pinaagi sa pagdala sa polen'.

Formic acid card: Cebuano body renders 'ants' as 'langgam', which is BIRD in Cebuano (Tagalog false friend). Reads 'Ang pipila ka langgam sama sa wood ants nagaspray og formic acid' and, fatally, 'gikan kini sa Latin nga formica nga nagpasabot og langgam' — so the card's entire point teaches that formica means bird. Never corrected in the body; only title_bis ('Hulmigas ug Asido') has the right word.

Plant bulb rendered 'bombilya', which in Cebuano means an electric light bulb. The card then says roots grow down from its flat base and leaves grow up — a child reads that a light bulb grows roots and leaves. Nothing in the card (title_bis is only 'Gamot Paubos Dahon Pataas') names the plant structure, so the actual subject is unrecoverable. Correct sense would be the onion/garlic-type bulb (e.g. 'bonggolan'/'ang bulb sa tanom sama sa sibuyas').

'ants' translated as 'langgam', which in Cebuano means BIRD (the Tagalog false friend: TL langgam = ant, CEB langgam = bird). Card says the pangolin's sticky tongue catches 'langgam ug termite ilawom sa yuta' — birds and termites underground. The card never restores 'ants' (Cebuano 'hulmigas'), and elsewhere in this same corpus 'langgam' is used correctly for birds, so the child has no way to recover the fact.

Unit changed: English '2,300 acres' becomes '2,300 ka ektarya' (hectares). 2,300 acres is about 930 hectares, so the Cebuano overstates the honey fungus's area by ~2.5x. Number-with-unit is the whole point of the card and is not corrected anywhere.

title_bis 'Bakuna nga Hilanat ug Rash' says VACCINE (bakuna) causes the fever and rash. The card is about chickenpox (bulutong-tubig) causing fever before the blisters — no vaccine is involved. Title-level defect with a health-misinformation reading ('vaccines give you fever and rash'); body uses 'bulutong-tubig' correctly, but the title as displayed names the wrong thing.

title_bis 'Gasgas sa Card sa Tuko' — 'tuko' is a gecko in Cebuano, not a stinger. English title is 'Scrape Out the Stinger'; the body correctly uses 'tibo sa buyog' (bee stinger), so the title names an animal that has nothing to do with the card (likely a mangling of 'tusok'/'tibo').

Body opens "Ang mga gapnod o liana mokatay paibabaw sa mga kahoy" — `gapnod` is driftwood/water-borne debris, not a vine (Cebuano is `balagon`, or `baging`). The card names a different thing as its lead noun and `gapnod` is also seeded into `terms` alongside `baging`, so retrieval carries the bad pairing too. Partial mitigation: title_bis is correctly "Mga Baging" and `liana` is kept in-line, so the climbing-for-canopy-light fact itself survives — flagging mainly because the wrong-word pair is corpus-wide greppable and was written into terms on purpose.

title_bis 'Pagliko sa Alupihan' names the centipede, but the card is about a millipede coiling into a spiral. The corpus consistently uses 'alupihan' for centipede and leaves millipede in English (ffct-01041 contrasts 'millipede ug alupihan'; ffct-09946 'Ang alupihan adunay usa ka paris nga tiil sa matag segment'). The Cebuano body never supplies a Cebuano name, so the title is uncorrected and teaches that a centipede is the animal that curls up - the exact trait that separates millipedes from centipedes.

EN: "Why does your tummy rumble when you're hungry?" BIS renders rumble as "magkalibang" twice: "Nganong magkalibang ang tiyan kon gutom?" ... "mao nga magkalibang ang tiyan". In this corpus kalibang always means defecate/diarrhea (58 hits, e.g. ffct-00355 "Kon ang bata magkalibang o magsuka", ffct-02996 "Rason sa Kalibang"). Every other stomach-growl card uses mosaba / mongulob / mokuros / mokabog / nagpakagol (ffct-04401, ffct-11180, ffct-14596, ffct-12944). A Cebuano-only child reads that an empty stomach makes you move your bowels; the rumbling-sound fact is never delivered anywhere on the card.

title_bis "Sakit sa Baba" (mouth pain/illness) for title_en "Jaw Joint Chewing". The card is pure anatomy — a joint in front of the ear that moves the apapangig up, down and sideways so you can chew and speak — and never mentions pain or disease. Using "Baba" for jaw is a corpus title convention (ffct-14407 "Molars sa Baba", ffct-14495 "Honey Badger sa Baba"), so the defect is "Sakit": all 25 other "Sakit ..." titles in the corpus sit on English titles that really are about pain or disease, making this one the lone outlier that renames the card's topic.

title_bis "Lihog sa Kangkong" for "Kangkong Stems". Lihog/palihog means please/a favour, not stem; the body correctly uses "punoan". Same wrong mapping recurs corpus-wide in exactly the stem slot — ffct-01646 "Tubig sa Lihog" (Water in Stems) and ffct-37862 "Gibag-on sa Lihog" (Stem Thickness) — so it is one lexicon entry, not a typo, and a single fix covers 3 titles. Title-only; the body of each card still delivers the fact, so treat as lower severity than the two above.

Types-of-teeth card. EN: "pointy canines for tearing". BIS: "hait nga canines para mopunit" — `punit` is to pick up / gather (corpus-wide it is used only that way: "pagpunit ug basura", "napunit nga palay", "mopunit og bato"), not to tear (`mogisi`). The card lists one job per tooth type (cut / tear / crush-grind) and nothing else in the Cebuano restores tearing, so a child reading only the Cebuano learns canines are for picking things up.

title_bis "Tiil nga Lambay" for EN title "Webbed Feet". `lambay` is the swimming crab in Cebuano — elsewhere in this same corpus it is used exactly that way ("Ang kugita mokaon og lambay, pasayan, ug kinhason"). The title therefore reads "crab feet" on a card about ducks. The body does give the right term ("tiil nga may lapyahan tali sa mga tudlo"), so this is a title-only defect, flagged because it names a different animal in the title.

Egret is rendered `bakaw`, which in Cebuano is the mangrove tree (`bakaw`/`bakhaw`/`bakawan` — used that way ~170x elsewhere in this same corpus, e.g. ffct-00444, ffct-01680). The card never says `langgam`, so nothing restores the referent: a child reads "ang mga bakaw ... kan-on nila ang insekto, ulod, ug peste sa humayan" as mangroves eating insects in rice fields. The corpus's own words for egret/heron are tulabong/talabong/tagak (ffct-00713, ffct-09030). title_bis has the same problem plus Tagalog `magsasaka`.

title_bis "Yugto sa Hantak" for "Caterpillar Stage" — `hantak` is not caterpillar (it is the coin-toss gambling game; caterpillar is `ulod`, which the body correctly uses). The heading names a different thing than the card. Greps clean: only 2 corpus hits, both caterpillar titles (this card and ffct-07873, titled just "Hantak"), so both are wrong. Body still delivers the fact, so title-only severity.

title_bis "Fovea Matarong" renders "sharp" as `matarong` = righteous/upright — wrong property, not a register choice. The body uses the correct `pinaka-hait`, so the fact survives; the heading does not. Grep is clean and all hits are the same error: ffct-02597 "Matarong nga Ngipon sa Karniboro" (Sharp Teeth of Meat Eaters) and ffct-32728 "Obsidian nga Matarong" (Sharp Obsidian).

title_bis "Tulo ka Nutrient sa Bali" renders "balance" as `bali`, which in Cebuano means a fracture/break — the same corpus uses `bali` with exactly that meaning in bone cards (ffct-00710 "Ang fracture mao ang bali o liki sa bukog", ffct-02434, ffct-09258). A child reads the heading as "three nutrients for a broken bone". Body is correct and complete, so title-only; same swap recurs in ffct-01096, ffct-01346, ffct-10261, ffct-12116.

MEDIUM. EN: "When ready to lay eggs, a female hornbill enters a tree hole and seals the entrance." BIS: "Kung manguhog na, mosulod ang baye nga kalaw sa lungag sa kahoy ug isirhan ang agianan, mao nga makulong kini sa sulod." The trigger the card exists for -- she is about to LAY EGGS (mangitlog) -- is replaced by 'manguhog', built on uhog (mucus/snot); the corpus itself uses uhog for mucus (ffct-13399, snail slime) and mangitlog 224x for egg-laying. So the Cebuano answer to its own question "Ngano gisirhan sa baye nga kalaw ang iyang kaugalingon?" collapses into a circular 'she seals the entrance so she is shut inside', with no egg/nesting reason left in the body; title_bis 'Salag sa Hornbill' gives nest but never eggs. 'manguhog' occurs exactly once in the entire sweep corpus -- this card -- so it is a one-off corruption, not a regional form.

LOW/PLAUSIBLE, title-only. title_en "Marang Spoils Quickly" -> title_bis "Marang nga Dali Mabuak" = marang breaks/cracks easily, a different (and false-sounding-plausible) claim about the fruit. Corpus usage is unambiguous: buak/mabuak = break, crack, smash across 236 cards (parrot beaks cracking seeds, hollow bird bones, blood vessels bursting). The body does restore the real fact ("Ang marang dali ra madaot"), so this is recoverable -- I raise it only because the gold set treats a title that states a different thing (e.g. ffct-15087 'asin' for smoke) as a flag even when the body is right.

LOW/PLAUSIBLE, title-only. title_en "Parents Give Half Each" -> title_bis "Gene sa Kadungganan"; kadungganan is honor/dignity (dungog), not katunga (half), so the title a child sees reads 'gene of honor'. Not idiosyncratic to this card: the same corruption is in ffct-24601, title_bis "Kadungganan sa String" for title_en "Halving String Jumps Pitch" -- both cards are about halves, and those two are the only occurrences of kadungganan in the corpus. The body is correct ("ang matag ginikanan naghatag og katunga sa mga gene sa anak"), so the fact is recoverable from the card.

EN question is about a lizard ("Why does a lizard feel warm in the sun?"); BIS asks about `halas` = snake ("Ngano nga moinit ang lawas sa halas sa adlaw?"). Different animal, never corrected anywhere on the card (title `Bugnaw og Dugo`, terms have only `reptilya`), so the Cebuano-only reader is pointed at the wrong creature — and at the likely lizard illustration. The cold-blooded claim itself stays true, so this is a wrong-referent defect rather than a false fact.

Rafflesia card. EN: the stink attracts flies "that help pollinate it". BIS: "...makadani og mga langaw nga motabang sa pagpamulak niini" — pagpamulak = flowering/blooming, not pollination. The card's whole point (flies act as pollinators) is replaced by a false mechanism (flies make it bloom), and nothing else in the Cebuano card mentions pollen or polinasyon, so it is unrecoverable. Other cards in this same batch correctly use 'polinasyon' / 'mabalhin ang pollen' (ffct-13678, ffct-13686).

Bulb-plant card. EN: "Onion and garlic aren't the only bulb plants — lily and tulip make bulbs too!" BIS: "Dili lang sibuyas ug ahos ang naghimo og bombilya — mao usab ang liryo ug tulip!" bombilya is an electric light bulb, not the plant bulb (bulbo). The Cebuano body names a different thing and never restores it; title_bis keeps only the bare English word 'Bulb' ("Lily ug Tulip sa Bulb"), which a grade-5 reader will most likely map to the same light bulb. Reads as: onions and garlic make light bulbs.

Queen ANT card turned into a bird card and never corrected. bis: "Ngano nga mas dako ang reyna kaysa mga trabahante nga LANGGAM?" and title_bis "Reyna sa Langgam" (= Queen of the Birds) for title_en "The Bigger Queen Ant". In Cebuano langgam = bird (hulmigas/subay/hantik = ant); the word 'ant' appears nowhere in the Cebuano, and the wing detail ("didto kaniadto nakakabit ang iyang mga pako") makes the bird reading fully coherent, so a child reads a false fact about birds. Tagalog-interference (Tg langgam = ant).

The sentence carrying the card's whole contrast says BIRDS: "dili na kini mahimo sa mga hamtong nga LANGGAM" for EN "the grown-up ants can't spin silk anymore". The question/title do say hantik, but the payload clause names a different animal, so the larvae-vs-adult-ant contrast (the fact the card exists for) is lost / turned into a claim about adult birds.

title_bis "Alibangbang ug Kagaw" = "Butterfly and GERM" for title_en "Butterfly vs Moth Rest". Corpus confirms kagaw = germ (e.g. ffct-01879 "Hugasi ang Kagaw"/Wash Away Germs, ffct-03167 "Kagaw sa Kamot"/Germs on Hands) and that moth = anunugba/gamu-gamo (ffct-03405, ffct-01201). The body only uses the English word "moth", so the Cebuano never restores it — the title teaches moth = kagaw. Same defect recurs at ffct-03195 ("Kagaw Makadungog Paniki"/Moths Hear Bats).

title_bis "Langgam sa Linya" = "Birds in a Line" for title_en "Ants Follow Scent Lines". The body is correct ("ang mga subay molakaw nga sunod-sunod..."), but the displayed title names a different animal than the card, mirroring the known iro/cat title defect; same ant->langgam slip also at ffct-00110 and ffct-01426.

Dietary-fiber card ends "malikayan ang tibi". In Cebuano `tibi` is the everyday word for TB (tuberculosis); constipation is Tagalog `tibi`. A Cebuano-only reader gets the false health claim "fiber prevents TB", and nothing in the card restores "hard stool / constipation" — the surrounding text only says fiber helps the large intestine move waste. The corpus's other constipation card (ffct-10342) keeps the English word "constipation" in the Cebuano, so this rendering is unique to this card (one grep hit corpus-wide, so low blast radius).

EN says the body's cells number in the trillions; bis says "ang tanan sa binilyon nga selula" = billions, a 1000x understatement of the number. The card contradicts itself: title_bis is "Trilyon Selusa Usa" while the body says binilyon, so a child reading only the Cebuano gets two conflicting magnitudes and the stated number in the body text is simply wrong. Should be "trilyon".

title_bis "Langgam Bati Yanig" — in Cebuano `langgam` means BIRD (it is Tagalog that uses langgam for ant). The card is entirely about ants (body correctly says `hulmigas`), so the Cebuano title names a different animal: "Bird Feels Vibration". Same class of defect as the cat card titled `iro`. The terms list confirms the slip: `langgam` is listed on the Tagalog side and `hulmigas` on the Cebuano side.

title_bis "2.5 Milyon Langgam Tawo" — again `langgam` (Cebuano = bird) used for ants; body correctly says `hulmigas` and the terms row pairs Tagalog `langgam at tao` with Cebuano `hulmigas ug tawo`. A Cebuano child reads the headline as "2.5 million birds" for an ants-vs-people card.

"giant clams" rendered `tahong` in both title_bis ("Tubbataha Gigante nga Tahong") and body ("dagkong tahong"). `Tahong` is the green mussel, a different bivalve; the giant clam is `taklobo` in Cebuano — and card ffct-14477 in this same batch uses `taklobo` correctly. Nothing in the card corrects it, so the child learns Tubbataha is known for giant mussels rather than giant clams.

Ants card: the Cebuano question and body use `langgam`, which is BIRD in Cebuano (Tagalog interference — Tagalog langgam = ant). Q: `Giunsa pag-ambit sa pagkaon sa mga langgam?` and `...baba ngadto sa baba sa laing langgam`. A Cebuano child reads a card about birds sharing food mouth-to-mouth in a colony; the body never corrects it (only the title `Hulmigas` and the untranslated English `worker ant` hint at ants). Sibling card ffct-14661 uses `hulmigas` correctly, confirming the corpus norm.

title_bis 'Tiki nga Layag' names the sailfin lizard a tiki (house gecko) — a different animal. The Cebuano body never corrects it: it keeps the English 'sailfin lizard' and gives no Cebuano name, and the card's own terms list carries the correct 'ibid'. A child reading only the Cebuano learns that the protected animal is a house gecko.
